passage: Note from Avni, school counsellor. At Thursday's parent meeting, Jomon sat with his son Rohit's report and said, more than once, "The neighbour's boy already has a rank in the top ten. Why can't he do the same?" His jaw was tight, and he kept turning his pen. When I asked what he was hoping for, he said, "I wanted to study engineering and never could. I don't want Rohit to end up behind like me." He looked surprised at his own words. I asked what Rohit hears when he says it. After a pause, Jomon said, "Probably that he isn't enough." What I did: I suggested he name one thing Rohit really worked at, and he mentioned the neat maths notebook Rohit had kept up for a month. He wrote it down to say at home.

qa.q: What did Jomon say the neighbour's boy already had?
qa.a: He said the neighbour's boy already had a rank in the top ten.

qa.q: What was Jomon afraid of when he compared Rohit to the neighbour's boy?
qa.a: He was afraid Rohit would fall behind as he felt he had, and his own regret over engineering sat under the comparison.

qa.q: What could Jomon do at home that would motivate Rohit better than comparing?
qa.a: He could praise real effort, such as the neat maths notebook, so Rohit knows his father sees the work he does.

qa.q: How might Rohit feel hearing his father's comparison?
qa.a: Probably that he isn't enough, as Jomon himself guessed, which could make love feel conditional on results.

grounding: Shows a parent comparing his child from fear and regret, seen by a counsellor who helps him notice and praise real effort.
